We are living through the convergence of two worlds – the consumer devices collecting and relaying our data, and the regulated devices once sold only through clinicians – all powered by the AI that links them. The Device Files Summit gathers the people shaping how that future unfolds.

01

Consumer Tech

The phones, wearables, and sensors now collecting and relaying continuous data from everyday life – and the AI models turning that raw stream into something intelligent.

02

Regulated Medicine

The clinicians, regulators, and medical devices that once lived only inside the clinic – holding the standards of evidence, safety, and care that consumer signals must now rise to meet.

03

The Quantified Self

The new default: health measured not once a year, but every moment – and the questions of agency, equity, and access that follow.

04

AI in Health

The models and systems that can extend a stretched workforce – triaging, monitoring, and guiding – to help close care gaps and ease clinical shortages, so expertise reaches the people and places that go without.

Not a conference

A gathering, not an audience.

Most events are broadcast: a stage, a crowd, a queue for the microphone. The Device Files Summit is built on the opposite premise.

Everyone here participates. There are no passive seats. Each person is selected because of what they'll contribute to the room – whether that's leading a session, provoking a debate, or bringing a perspective no one else can.

We keep it small on purpose. One day, one shared table, and a group carefully composed to hold the most honest conversation of the year about where continuous health is headed.

50participants, each with a role to play – no observers, no back row
3days to gather — a welcome reception the first afternoon, a full day of programming, then breakfast and a choice of alpine excursion to close
100%of the room composed by hand, to balance discipline, seniority, and viewpoint

How participation works

A curated convergence

We're aiming to fill the room with thoughtful leaders across a variety of backgrounds, experiences, and countries – whether from industry, services, nonprofits, or government. We don't sell tickets; we compose a room of participants.

Step 01

Submit an inquiry

Tell us who you are. A few thoughtful questions – not a résumé – help us understand the perspective you'd add to the table.

Step 02

Curation

We assemble the group deliberately, balancing founders, clinicians, regulators, investors, and researchers so every session has the right minds in it.

Step 03

Invitation

Selected participants receive an invitation – and we'll discuss your desired level of participation, from discussion leader to engaged audience.

The setting

Kempinski Palace Engelberg

A restored Belle Époque palace beneath Mount Titlis – a luxury first five-star hotel, forty minutes from Lucerne and a world away from the everyday.

The hotel

A Belle Époque palace in the Alps

A restored 1900s grand hotel, wrapped in contemporary luxury beneath Mount Titlis.

A five-star, restored Belle Époque palace – the Kempinski Palace sits in the heart of Engelberg, beneath Mount Titlis.

Belle Époque architecture opens into rooms of quiet grandeur with views straight onto the peaks. The Cattani restaurant carries the day from first coffee to final toast, and the Titlis cable car begins minutes from the door.

Thanks to straightforward trains from Basel, Geneva, Zürich, and even Milan, Engelberg has become a favorite all-season mountain escape – particularly for ski weekends combining Titlis’ high-alpine terrain with the comforts of a luxury hotel.

Interalpen-Hotel Tyrol

The hotel

A five-star Austrian retreat

Chalet-inspired in wood and stone, wrapped in Tyrolean forest at 1,300 metres.

The Interalpen-Alm

A hut in the forest, a world of its own

A ten-minute walk from the hotel, the Interalpen mountain hut waits among the pines – panelled wood, a traditional stove, and the warmth of a true Tyrolean experience. This is where the summit gathers.

Few places on earth combine total seclusion with total ease. The Interalpen sits alone on a high plateau, wrapped in the Tyrolean forest outside of Innsbruck, near the famous Olympiaregion Seefeld.

This family-owned, five-star chalet-inspired hotel boasts architecture in wood and stone that opens into rooms of surprising grandeur. A 5,300 m² spa unfolds across a sauna village, panoramic pools, and forest views. Michelin-recognized kitchens carry the day from first coffee to final toast. Cross-country ski trails begin at the door.

On the table

Topics we may explore

A sample of the questions this room is built to move forward – illustrative, not exhaustive, and never a fixed agenda. The final sessions take shape with our founding participants.

Topic 01

Who owns the first conversation

The wearable now notices the change – HRV drift, a sleep pattern, a blood-pressure trend – before the patient or the doctor does. Whoever interprets that signal inherits the first conversation in healthcare, and the spending that follows it. What happens to the physician's role, and to the patient's trust?

Topic 02

One roof: monitoring, interpretation, routing, billing

A single company can now detect a signal, interpret it with AI, route you to a program, and bill for it. Physicians are barred from self-referral; platforms are not. Is this the efficiency the system needs – or a patient-trust and antitrust question we haven't named?

Topic 03

When attention logic meets clinical judgment

Wearables were built to optimize engagement and monetize data. Now that same optimization is steering clinical decisions – which specialist, which program, which subscription. Who owns the most intimate record we've ever produced, and whose interest does the nudge serve?

Topic 04

The end of the wellness exemption

Regulators are lowering the barrier for some devices while closing the 'wellness' cover for medical-grade claims. Wellness versus medical device is now a strategic choice made at the whiteboard, not discovered in a warning letter. Where's the line, and who draws it?

Topic 05

Consumer tech is now MedTech

The moment a device detects, monitors, or manages, it crosses into medical territory – and strategy, evidence, and leadership all have to align around that. Is this the identity shift the whole field is trying to name?

Topic 06

Funding the convergence

AI and direct-to-consumer move at one speed; regulated medicine at another. This future needs early-stage investors fluent in both at once – comfortable with consumer velocity and clinical rigor in the same thesis. How do we educate investors to get comfortable investing at this convergence?

Topic 07

Who pays for continuous care

Monitoring only becomes care if someone funds the response to it. Reimbursement still rewards legacy volume, yet outcome-based pathways are beginning to open. Does continuous data lower total cost – or just add spend?

Topic 08

From clearance to standard of care

Breakthrough status is not a path to patients. Between coverage, EHR integration, and clinical workflow, the system loses most of what it approves. Where does it actually break?

Topic 09

Where the system places risk

As judgment shifts from clinician to algorithm to the person wearing the device, who is the backstop when it's wrong? If the physician is no longer the sole safety check, the system has to decide – deliberately – where accountability now sits.

Topic 10

AI as the accelerant

AI is what forces regulators to treat a wearable as more than a sensor – an interpretive engine that shapes care. Is AI the thing that finally makes wearables medicine, and can it extend a stretched clinical workforce without breaking trust?

A starting set, not a final one – founding participants help shape the questions and the sessions.
